p01.question: A slide reads “94.7% accuracy, ready for launch”. What is the most useful question to ask?
options: Which algorithm produced that number, and can we try a stronger one
What decision does this prediction drive, and what does each kind of mistake cost us
How long did training take and how much did the compute cost
Can the team get it above 97% before we commit to a date
p01.explanation: Accuracy alone says nothing about the product. The decision and the cost of each error direction are what determine the threshold, the metric to optimise and whether the feature is worth shipping — and they are the product manager's to supply, not the team's.

p01.question: Why is “the model must not make mistakes” an acceptance criterion no team can satisfy?
options: Because models are new technology and will improve later
Because the training data always contains errors
Because a working model is wrong on a known share of cases by design, so the criterion has to name how often and in which direction
Because mistakes can only be counted after a full year of operation
p01.explanation: Being wrong is not a defect to be removed; it is a property of a probabilistic system. A criterion that forbids it can never be met, so the team will quietly reinterpret it instead of telling you — which is worse than an honest error budget.

p01.question: Fraud is 0.8% of transactions. A model answers “not fraud” every single time. What does accuracy report?
options: 99.2%, and it catches nothing — accuracy hides how rare the event is
0.8%, because it misses every fraud case
50%, because there are two possible answers
It cannot be computed without a threshold
p01.explanation: With a rare event the majority answer scores brilliantly while being useless. This is the single most common way an impressive number survives a review it should not have survived.

p01.question: A model outputs 0.83 that a transaction is fraud. Who decides whether 0.83 blocks the payment?
options: The model — the threshold is part of its training
The ML engineer, since it is a technical parameter
Nobody: 0.5 is the industry standard and is used as is
The product manager, because moving it trades one cost against another
p01.explanation: The threshold decides how many honest customers you block in order to catch how much fraud. That is a business trade with money on both sides, not a technical default — and 0.5 is a default nobody chose.

p01.question: The team reports a strong offline metric. What does that entitle you to say?
options: That the feature is ready for release
That the candidate is worth an experiment on live traffic
That the business metric will improve by a similar margin
That the model will hold its quality for at least a year
p01.explanation: Offline numbers filter candidates; only an experiment on real traffic tells you what the feature does to the business. Treating the filter as the verdict is how features ship that look good and change nothing.

p02.question: “Block an order over 100,000 if the account is less than a day old.” Rule or model?
options: A model — fraud patterns change constantly
A model, because the amount threshold should be learned from data
A rule — the condition is a complete sentence, it is stable, and every block can be explained
Neither: the request needs to be rejected as too risky
p02.explanation: Written down, the condition is complete and checkable, and it does not drift. It also has to be explainable to the blocked customer, which pushes further toward a rule. Days of work instead of weeks, and auditable by anyone.

p02.question: Which signal says a rule has outlived itself and the problem has become model-shaped?
options: It needs a new exception nearly every week and nobody can predict the next one
It has grown past fifty lines of code
A competitor has announced they use machine learning for it
The team finds it boring to maintain
p02.explanation: Length is not the signal — edit frequency is. Unpredictable weekly exceptions mean the condition is no longer knowable in advance, which is exactly what a model is for. Usefully, the exception log you have been keeping is your labelled training data.

p02.question: Which set of costs does a first sprint estimate for a model typically leave out?
options: Server capacity and the cost of the programming language
Design review and copywriting
The price of the training data licence only
Data that exists at decision time, weeks rather than days, permanent upkeep, and the burden of explaining an answer
p02.explanation: None of these show up in the first sprint, and all of them are permanent. The upkeep in particular never ends: someone owns retraining, monitoring and the pager for as long as the feature lives.

p02.question: “Email anyone who has not opened the app in 30 days.” What is the right response?
options: A model, since predicting app opens requires learning from behaviour
The email itself is a rule; the interesting problem hiding inside it is choosing whom it is worth contacting
A rule, and there is no further question worth asking
Decline it: mass email is not a product feature
p02.explanation: The trigger is trivially a rule. The valuable reframing is that whom to contact — and with what offer — is a churn problem a model already solves. Finding the better question inside a weak request is most of the job.

p02.question: What makes “we are not using ML for that” land as a decision rather than a refusal?
options: Citing the team's capacity for the quarter
Escalating to the CTO so the answer carries authority
Offering the faster alternative and naming the condition that would make you revisit — and owning the watch for it
Promising to reconsider it next planning cycle
p02.explanation: A comparison gives the requester something now; a named trigger shows the decision is reversible on evidence rather than on rank; taking the watch yourself means they do not have to keep pushing. Capacity is true but sounds like a queue.

p03.question: A stakeholder asks for “a model that makes our search smarter”. What has to be filled in before this can enter a roadmap?
options: A budget and a target launch date
A decision on which model architecture to use
The four slots: what the prediction is about, at what moment it is made, which decision it changes, and who acts on it
A benchmark taken from a competitor's search
p03.explanation: “Smarter” is a wish, not a specification. Until the object, the moment, the decision and the actor are named, there is nothing for a team to build and nothing for you to measure — and no way to tell whether the result was worth the quarter.

p03.question: Which of these is stated as a decision rather than a wish?
options: When the results page renders, we re-rank the top 50 candidates, and the customer sees a different order
Search should understand what the customer means
Search relevance should improve quarter over quarter
We should use embeddings to represent queries
p03.explanation: A decision says what changes, for whom, and at what moment. The second and third options describe a desirable state with no action attached; the fourth is an implementation choice, which is the team's to make, not the brief's.

p03.question: A team ships a model whose output appears only on an internal dashboard that nobody has the authority to act on. What has gone wrong?
options: The model is not accurate enough to be trusted
The dashboard needs better visual design
The predictions should have been written to a database instead
No decision was attached to the prediction, so the model changes nothing however good it is
p03.explanation: This is the dashboard failure mode. A prediction with no decision behind it produces a number somebody looks at, not an outcome. Accuracy is irrelevant here: at 99% it would still change nothing.

p03.question: Why does “at what moment” matter as much as “what do we predict”?
options: Because the model has to be retrained on that schedule
Because the moment fixes which data exists yet and how much latency the prediction is allowed
Because it determines which team owns the feature
Because predictions made at the wrong time of day are less accurate
p03.explanation: The moment is a hard constraint on both sides. It decides which features are legitimately available (module P4's point-in-time trap) and what the latency budget is — a prediction that needs 400 ms cannot sit in a path that has 50.

p03.question: Three framings of “make search smarter” are on the table and one of them can be shipped as a rule. Why start there?
options: It delivers the decision and the interface change immediately, and it becomes the baseline the model has to beat
Because rules are always more accurate than models on search problems
Because the ML team is busy with other work this quarter
Because rules need no data
p03.explanation: Shipping the rule first tests the part most likely to be wrong — that anyone acts differently because of the prediction — at a fraction of the cost. It also produces the number the model will be judged against, which is the subject of module P10.

p04.question: A feature is about to enter the roadmap. Which unanswered data question most often kills it later?
options: Whether the data is stored in the same format across systems
Whether the label — the thing you want to predict — is recorded anywhere at all
Whether the warehouse has enough disk space
Whether the data is refreshed daily or hourly
p04.explanation: Features are usually plentiful and labels are not. A project with inputs but no recorded outcome has no way to learn, and discovering that after the commitment turns a quarter into a data-collection project nobody scheduled.

p04.question: At checkout you want to predict whether a delivery will be late. Which of these fields may NOT be used as a feature?
options: The customer's city, taken from the order
The courier's average delay over the previous month
The number of items in the basket
The warehouse dispatch time, which is recorded two hours after the order is placed
p04.explanation: The dispatch time does not exist at checkout, so the live model would never have it. Training on it produces an excellent offline score and a useless production model — the point-in-time trap, and the most common cause of a result that does not survive launch.

p04.question: What does “the label may come from the future, but the features may not” mean in practice?
options: You learn the answer after the fact, which is fine; but every input must have existed at the moment the prediction is made
Labels should be collected before any features are engineered
Historical data is unusable for training and only live data counts
Features have to be recomputed every time a new label arrives
p04.explanation: That asymmetry is the whole rule. The outcome is by definition known later — that is what makes it a label. The inputs are bound to the moment of the decision, and any that are not leak information the model will not have in production.

p04.question: Which label source is usually the cheapest and the most trustworthy, when it exists?
options: Manual annotation by a contracted team
A label inferred by another model
An outcome the product already records as a side effect of normal operation
A survey sent to customers after the fact
p04.explanation: A refund, a cancellation, a click, a chargeback — the product writes these down anyway, at full volume and without anyone's opinion in the middle. Annotation costs money per item and carries the annotator's judgement; a model-inferred label teaches the new model the old model's mistakes.

p04.question: The data exists for 30% of orders — the ones placed through the mobile app. What follows?
options: The project is impossible and should be cancelled
You can safely extrapolate the model to the other 70%
Coverage does not matter as long as the sample is large enough
The feature can launch for mobile orders only, and that limit belongs in the brief rather than in a post-launch surprise
p04.explanation: Partial coverage is a scope statement, not a blocker. What makes it dangerous is discovering it after the promise: the model has simply never seen the other channel, so its numbers there are unknown rather than merely worse.

p05.question: What is the three-metric chain?
options: A business metric, an online proxy you can move within a test, and an offline metric the team optimises — each linked to the one above it
Accuracy, precision and recall, always reported together
A daily, a weekly and a monthly dashboard
One metric per team: product, engineering and finance
p05.explanation: The chain exists because the metric that matters moves too slowly to steer by and the metric the team can optimise means nothing to the business. The proxy in the middle is what connects a model improvement to a result somebody cares about.

p05.question: Why is accuracy a poor KPI for a product review?
options: Because it is hard to compute reliably
Because executives do not understand percentages
Because nobody outside the team can act on it, and it can rise while the business metric falls
Because it changes every time the model is retrained
p05.explanation: Accuracy is an internal instrument, useful to the team tuning the model. As a KPI it hides which error got better, and a model can gain a point of accuracy by becoming more cautious in exactly the cases that made money.

p05.question: Treating the chain as “a testable claim” means what?
options: The chain is validated by asking more stakeholders whether they agree
You are asserting that moving the offline metric moves the proxy, and the proxy moves the business metric — and an experiment can prove you wrong
Each metric has to be tested by a separate team
The chain should be rewritten every quarter regardless of results
p05.explanation: Written down as a claim, the chain becomes falsifiable: if the offline metric improves and the proxy does not, the link is wrong and you have learned something real. Written down as a list of metrics, it just decorates the document.

p05.question: Why name one deciding number before the experiment runs?
options: Because finance requires a single figure for forecasting
Because more than one metric cannot be measured in the same test
Because a model can only be optimised against a single objective
Because deciding afterwards lets you pick whichever metric happened to move, which is how a failed test becomes a launch
p05.explanation: Naming it in advance is what makes the result binding. With five metrics and no commitment, something will always be up, and the review turns into a search for the friendliest chart rather than a decision.

p05.question: What is a guardrail metric for?
options: To replace the primary metric if that one does not move
To give every stakeholder a metric they own
To catch the damage a win might be hiding — it does not need to improve, it must not get worse
To measure the model's technical performance in production
p05.explanation: Guardrails exist because a feature can win on its own metric and lose overall: clicks up, revenue flat, complaints up. They are set as limits, not targets, and one of them breaking is a reason not to ship even when the primary number is good.

p06.question: Risk wants an aggressive fraud threshold, Support wants a conservative one. What settles the argument?
options: Whichever side escalates to the CTO first
Splitting the difference between the two proposals
A more accurate model, which removes the trade-off
A number on each of the two errors, so the trade can be calculated instead of argued
p06.explanation: Both sides are describing a real cost, so neither can win on conviction. A better model shifts the whole curve but never removes the choice: at any accuracy, some threshold still has to be picked, and that is a product decision made of two prices.

p06.question: What does moving the threshold actually do?
options: It makes the model more accurate at the cost of latency
It trades misses for false alarms — it cannot reduce both
It changes how often the model is retrained
It removes the need to price the errors
p06.explanation: The threshold does not touch the model's quality. It slides along a fixed trade-off, choosing which of the two mistakes you would rather make and how often — which is why it belongs to whoever owns the consequences, not to whoever trained the model.

p06.question: A threshold produces 900 alerts a day and the review team can handle 500. What is the effect?
options: The model catches 80% more fraud than it would at 500 alerts
The extra alerts are processed more slowly but remain useful
A backlog forms and the oldest alerts age past usefulness, so the extra 400 catch almost nothing
The review team's accuracy improves with volume
p06.explanation: Detection only counts once somebody acts on it. Past the team's capacity the queue grows without limit and alerts are reviewed after the money has moved, so the threshold is set by the cost ratio and the capacity to act together.

p06.question: How precise do the two error costs need to be?
options: An order of magnitude is usually enough — what matters is which way the asymmetry runs and roughly by how much
Accurate to the cent, or the threshold will be wrong
They need no numbers at all; a qualitative ranking is sufficient
They must be recalculated for every individual transaction
p06.explanation: When one error costs forty times the other, the second decimal place changes nothing and the ratio changes everything. A rough, written-down estimate also has a property that a qualitative ranking lacks: somebody can disagree with it and bring a better number.

p06.question: An error carries a serious safety or reputational consequence that cannot honestly be priced. What do you do?
options: Estimate a figure large enough to dominate the arithmetic
State that this error is not being traded against money, set a floor you will not ship above, and record it as a policy decision
Leave the threshold to the ML team, since it is no longer a product question
Drop the feature, because the trade-off cannot be computed
p06.explanation: An invented figure looks like analysis and can be renegotiated by anyone with a spreadsheet. A stated limit cannot: it says this is a constraint, not a variable. Module P18 works through how to document that.

p07.question: Why does estimating an ML feature differ from estimating an ordinary one?
options: Because ML teams work less predictably than other engineers
Because the central question — whether the data holds enough signal to change a decision — cannot be answered without doing part of the work
Because the time a model takes to train is impossible to measure
Because ML projects always overrun their plan
p07.explanation: On a normal feature the work is known and the risk is in execution. Here the answer does not exist yet, and nobody is withholding it. An estimate that ignores that is not an estimate — it is a promise somebody will be held to in November.

p07.question: Of the four stages of a typical ML project, which one is genuinely unbounded?
options: The data audit
Shipping the rule as a baseline
Productionisation — serving, monitoring, the fallback
The modelling
p07.explanation: The audit, the baseline and the productionisation estimate like ordinary engineering. Only the search for signal can eat a quarter, which is why it is the one stage that gets a cap instead of a date.

p07.question: What does a time-boxed spike deliver?
options: A decision by a fixed date, for a fixed budget
A trained model ready for production
An accuracy figure the team commits to
A complete PRD for the feature
p07.explanation: That is what makes a spike fundable: the CTO is not buying a model, he is buying an answer by a date, and he knows the price of the answer before it starts.

p07.question: Why must the stopping criterion be written before the work begins?
options: Because the team needs a target to optimise against
Because the budget has to be approved in advance
Because afterwards it stops being a criterion and becomes a negotiation — and the negotiation ends in two more weeks, every two weeks
Because it cannot be computed once a model exists
p07.explanation: Written early, it is a rule agreed by people with no attachment to the outcome. Written late, everyone in the room has three weeks invested in the answer, and the number moves to fit the work already done.

p07.question: Which kind of date can you always commit to the business?
options: The date the model reaches the target accuracy
The date the model goes to production
The date the project ends, with a buffer added for safety
The date on which you will know whether it works
p07.explanation: A decision date does not depend on the result, so it is always safe to promise. Delivery dates are safe only for the parts that do not depend on the search — the rule, the interface, the instrumentation.

p08.question: Why should the PRD not name the model family and the feature list?
options: Because the team will ignore that section anyway
Because it makes the document too long for executives
Because it locks the team out of anything better they find later, and leaves you defending a choice you have no way to defend
Because that information is commercially confidential
p08.explanation: The cost is paid twice: an amendment is needed before the team can adopt a better approach, and at the launch review the architecture is yours to justify. Neither is a trade a product manager should want.

p08.question: Which section does an ordinary PRD not have, while an ML PRD must?
options: A list of user stories
What the product does when the model is unsure, wrong, or unavailable
A competitive analysis
A target release date
p08.explanation: A model unsure about one case in six needs a defined behaviour for those cases, and every ML feature has a no-model mode whether or not anyone designed it. Leaving both out does not avoid the decision, it just makes it by default.

p08.question: What is wrong with “at least 90% accuracy” as an acceptance criterion?
options: 90% is too low a bar for a production feature
Accuracy cannot be measured before launch
It should be stated as precision and recall instead
It cannot be checked against anything a user sees, and a model that always predicts the common case can reach it while the feature does nothing
p08.explanation: Acceptance criteria have to be testable by someone who knows no machine learning. “No blocking error on timeout” and “every rejection is appealable in one click” qualify; a number that rises when the feature stays silent does not.

p08.question: Every ML feature has a mode in which no model is available. What decides what that mode looks like?
options: Whether you designed it — undesigned, it is an error page
The uptime guarantee of the serving infrastructure
How well the model's confidence is calibrated
Whether the model was trained on enough data
p08.explanation: Timeouts, rollbacks and outages are certainties, not risks. The only question is whether the product has a defined behaviour for them, and that behaviour is a product decision that belongs in your half of the document.

p08.question: The data exists only for mobile orders. Where does that belong in the PRD?
options: In the risks section, as something that might become a problem
Nowhere — it is an implementation detail for the team
In scope, as a stated coverage limit: mobile is in, web keeps the current behaviour
In the metrics section, as a caveat attached to the numbers
p08.explanation: Written as scope, it is a decision with a stated reason and a clear path to extending it. Left out, it becomes a broken promise discovered at launch by whoever expected the feature to cover their channel.

p09.question: A model returns a confidence value with every prediction. A feature that ignores that value —
options: treats a 0.51 exactly like a 0.99
is simpler, and therefore usually the better product decision
will be more accurate, because it acts on every case
cannot be A/B tested
p09.explanation: The confidence is the model's own admission of doubt, and it is the most valuable thing it produces beyond the answer itself. Throwing it away means the least reliable predictions reach the user dressed exactly like the most reliable ones.

p09.question: In the three-band design, which behaviour do product managers most often leave out?
options: Acting automatically on high confidence
Logging the prediction for later analysis
Routing the middle band to a human reviewer
Showing nothing at all
p09.explanation: Silence feels like a non-feature, so it gets dropped — and it is the band that saves you. Showing nothing returns the user to the experience that was acceptable last quarter, at the cases where the model is least worth trusting.

p09.question: Which wording is right for a delay advisory?
options: “Your order will be late.”
“Orders like this arrive late about 1 time in 4.”
“Our model predicts a delay with 78% confidence.”
“Warning: a delivery problem has been detected.”
p09.explanation: Describe the population, not the individual: a rate stays true when this particular order arrives on time. The confidence score is worse than it looks — it exposes an internal number the customer cannot act on, and still makes a claim about their order.

p09.question: What does a human reviewer need in order to be more than a rubber stamp?
options: The model's confidence score on every item
A monthly report on how often they agreed with the model
The evidence behind the flag, and a one-click way to disagree
Training in how the model works internally
p09.explanation: Given only a score, a reviewer has nothing to reason with and starts approving, which buys you an expensive random number generator. And if disagreeing is expensive, the queue quietly converges on whatever the model said.

p09.question: What rule follows from “a wrong prediction should cost the user a click, not a sale”?
options: No silent irreversible actions: either a human goes in front of it, or the reversal takes one click
The model must be retrained whenever a user complains
Automation is acceptable only for decisions with no user impact
The confidence threshold should be set as high as possible
p09.explanation: You will be wrong at a known rate, so the design question is what being wrong costs the person affected. An automated decision they cannot undo is not acceptable at any accuracy — and telling them a decision was made, and how to contest it, is often a legal duty as well.

p10.question: The team reports macro-F1 0.91. What makes that number meaningful?
options: Comparing it against accuracy figures published for similar tasks
Confirming it was computed on a properly held-out month
Asking whether it will hold up after the next retraining
Putting the other baselines next to it: do nothing, the shipped rule, a human
p10.explanation: Alone it is a number with no units. With the other bars the meeting changes question, from “is 0.91 good” to “are 7 points over the rule worth what the model costs to run” — which is answerable.

p10.question: Why is the already-shipped rule the most honest competitor for a model?
options: Because stakeholders find it easier to understand
Because rules are more robust to data drift
Because it already exists, costs nothing extra to run, and already delivers part of the value
Because it was built by the same team
p10.explanation: The model is not competing against perfection but against what is running today. Anything the rule already achieves is not a benefit of the model, which is why the increment — not the absolute score — is what is on trial.

p10.question: The model clears the spike's criterion by a comfortable margin. What follows?
options: It is a candidate; the decision still depends on what the increment is worth against what it costs to run
It should be productionised — the criterion was agreed in advance and met
The criterion was set too low and should be raised before deciding
The project can be declared a success and closed
p10.explanation: Clearing the criterion is the necessary condition. The sufficient one is money, including the cost of owning the model — and a model can beat its offline target, hit the PRD's business number, and still lose money every month.

p10.question: What is usually missing from “the model costs $1,900 a month in inference”?
options: The cost of the original training runs
Retraining, monitoring, on-call and the engineer-days for a new failure mode — together usually larger than inference
The product manager's own time
The discount available for committing to annual capacity
p10.explanation: Inference is the visible line on a cloud bill, so it is the one that gets quoted. The bill that decides the gate is the all-in cost of owning a model that must keep working, which module P15 prices properly.

p10.question: The spike ends with “we ship the rule and close the project”. How should that be written up?
options: As a failure, honestly, so that the organisation learns from it
Briefly and without numbers, so as not to draw attention to it
As a success, leaving out the model's numbers so nobody blames the team
As a success, with all four baselines shown and the specific number that would reopen the case
p10.explanation: The spike bought certainty in three weeks and freed a quarter, which is a win — but only if the memo says so. A team that learns an honest negative gets punished will bring you positive results for ever, and you will not be able to tell which are real.

p11.question: Of the four questions to ask about any evaluation, which one catches the most disasters?
options: Which algorithm produced the number
How many features the model uses
How the data was split into training and test
How long the training run took
p11.explanation: The split is where optimistic numbers are manufactured, and it takes no expertise to ask about. The other three questions matter, but this is the one whose wrong answer makes every other number on the slide meaningless.

p11.question: Eighteen months of transactions, split randomly 80/20. What is wrong with that?
options: Test cases sit surrounded by training data from the same week, so the model effectively sees the future — while production is always a split by time
A random split leaves the test set too small to be reliable
Nothing: random splitting is the standard approach for tabular data
The split should be 90/10 whenever the data is ordered in time
p11.explanation: Fraud, delays, churn and demand all arrive in waves, and a random split puts the same wave on both sides. In production the model is always asked about a day it has never seen, so an evaluation arranged any other way measures a situation that will never occur.

p11.question: The top features include “number of chargeback disputes for this customer”. What do you ask?
options: Whether more features like this one can be added
Whether this feature is correlated with the transaction amount
How much this feature contributes to the AUC
Whether, at the moment we score the payment, a dispute has been filed yet
p11.explanation: A dispute is filed days after the transaction, and for fraudulent transactions it is exactly what later gets disputed — so the model has been handed the answer. This is module P4's point-in-time rule applied to a feature-importance list, and asking it costs nothing.

p11.question: Why is “AUC 0.97” not a product statement?
options: Because AUC is only valid on balanced datasets
Because it averages over thresholds you will never use, while you ship exactly one — and the product needs precision and recall there, with the confusion matrix
Because AUC cannot be compared between two models
Because executives do not understand what it means
p11.explanation: “0.97 AUC” and “at our threshold it flags 500 a day, 60 of them real” describe the same model, and only the second can be used for anything — module P6's arithmetic cannot consume an AUC at all.

p11.question: The model is strong overall, and the feature will launch for mobile orders in three cities. What do you ask for?
options: Whether the model will be retrained after launch
Whether mobile orders were excluded from the training data
The same metric computed on mobile orders in those three cities
Whether the three cities carry enough traffic for an A/B test
p11.explanation: A model trained and evaluated on everything can be strong on average and weak exactly where you ship it. The number that matters is the number on the population that will actually meet the feature.

p12.question: What is the correct unit of randomisation for this experiment?
options: The prediction, because it yields the largest sample
The customer, held for the whole duration of the test
The session, so that behaviour is measured freshly each visit
The city, to keep the two groups geographically clean
p12.explanation: Randomising by session shows the same person the feature on Tuesday and not on Thursday; randomising per prediction means the groups are not groups. Both contaminate the comparison towards “no effect”, which is the worst kind of wrong because it looks like a clean negative.

p12.question: Group B loses the experiment. What have you actually learned?
options: That the model is not good enough and needs more training data
That the offline evaluation must have been wrong
That this bundle — model, threshold, copy and placement — is worse; which part is at fault is the next question, and it is usually not the model
That the feature should be abandoned
p12.explanation: The A/B compares experiences, not models. Treating a lost experiment as a verdict on the model is how a placement problem or a badly worded banner gets mistaken for a dead end.

p12.question: Slot changes are up 6%, revenue per visitor is down 2.1%, and both are outside their confidence intervals. Which do you believe?
options: Revenue — the proxy only ever existed as a hypothesis about revenue, and the experiment has just refuted the hypothesis
The proxy — it is measured more precisely and sits closer to the feature
Neither: the test is inconclusive and has to be re-run
Whichever of the two has the narrower confidence interval
p12.explanation: Clicks are not a small revenue. They were a claim that engagement with this feature would produce value, and the experiment tested that claim and rejected it. The proxy has no standing of its own once it stops predicting the thing that matters.

p12.question: The deciding number was met and a guardrail was broken. What do you do?
options: Ship — the primary metric is what everyone agreed would decide
Ship, and watch the guardrail closely after launch
Re-run the experiment with the guardrail set wider
Do not ship: the guardrail was written for exactly this case, a win that is hiding damage
p12.explanation: The whole value of a guardrail is that it was agreed before anyone had a result to defend. A breach outranks a hit on the primary metric — otherwise the guardrail was decoration and the pre-registration was theatre.

p12.question: Why fix the experiment's runtime in advance and then leave it alone?
options: Because the analytics platform charges per day of test
Because stopping when a number happens to look good promotes noise to a launch, and the opening days are distorted by novelty anyway
Because the model degrades if the test runs too long
Because longer tests reliably produce larger effects
p12.explanation: Peeking until something is significant guarantees that eventually something will be. And people react to anything new, so an effect measured in week one is partly a reaction to change rather than to value.

p13.question: What can shadow mode catch that offline evaluation structurally cannot?
options: A model that has overfitted its training data
A threshold set too low for the review team's capacity
Leakage from a feature that only exists after the decision
The live pipeline computing a feature differently from the way training computed it
p13.explanation: Offline evaluation uses the training pipeline's version of the inputs, so a mismatch between that and the live pipeline is invisible in every offline number. It is also the most common reason a model that scored well behaves oddly in production.

p13.question: What is the actual requirement for rollback?
options: A flag anyone on call can flip without an engineer, taking effect within a minute
A documented deploy procedure that completes in under an hour
A second model that can be swapped in as a replacement
The product manager's approval before the feature is switched off
p13.explanation: If switching the feature off needs a build and a deploy, your worst hour lasts forty minutes. And an off switch nobody at 3 a.m. feels authorised to use is not an off switch, so who may flip it is written down too.

p13.question: Which omission is cheap to fix today and impossible to fix in retrospect?
options: The hardcoded threshold that should be configurable
The shadow run that was skipped
Logging each prediction together with its inputs and the model version
The missing alert on the prediction rate
p13.explanation: Everything else on a launch checklist can be added later. Log lines cannot be back-filled: if the inputs and the version were never written down, the first serious complaint six weeks from now has no answer and never will.

p13.question: Why does the support team have to be briefed before the launch rather than after it?
options: Because support has to formally approve the feature
Because the people who will receive the complaints must know an automated decision exists before an angry customer tells them about it
Because support then explains the model's architecture to customers
Because the runbook requires a signature from every team
p13.explanation: One page and thirty minutes prevents an entirely self-inflicted incident. What it needs to contain is what the feature does, what it looks like when it is wrong, how a customer appeals, and the exact sentence to say.

p13.question: The experiment already ran three weeks on live traffic through the real serving pipeline. Does a shadow stage still add anything?
options: No — that stage's question has already been answered, and naming which step answered it is part of the decision
Yes — every launch has to pass all three stages in order
Yes — shadow mode is the only way to measure accuracy in production
No — shadow mode stops being useful once an A/B test has been designed
p13.explanation: Demanding the stage here is ceremony. But the reason has to be said out loud, or somebody concludes the stage is optional in general — and the next model that goes live without an experiment genuinely needs it.

p14.question: Why can production monitoring not be built on accuracy?
options: Because accuracy is not a business metric
Because accuracy requires a labelled test set and production has none
Because the outcome arrives days or months later, so accuracy is blind during exactly the window when something is going wrong
Because accuracy is too noisy to read at daily granularity
p14.explanation: Two days for a delivery, forty-five for a chargeback, ninety for churn. Accuracy is the truest signal and always the latest one, which makes it good for confirming a diagnosis and useless as an alarm.

p14.question: Which number is the fastest warning that the world has moved?
options: The weekly business metric
Service error rate and latency
Accuracy computed on matured labels
The share of cases the model acts on, daily — if it moves with no release, the world moved
p14.explanation: It is visible the same minute, costs nothing to compute, and needs no labels. In the situation this module opens with, it was the missing line: a third of orders quietly losing the feature moved it by a third, in week six.

p14.question: A courier identifier that never appeared in the training data arrives in production. What should the system do?
options: Predict using the average, which is the safest available estimate
Produce no prediction — the silent band — and raise the input-health number
Retrain automatically as soon as the new value is seen
Reject the order until somebody maps the new value
p14.explanation: A model that answers confidently with the average looks healthy on every dashboard while doing nothing, which is how eleven weeks pass unnoticed. A feature that fails visibly is worth far more than one that fails quietly.

p14.question: What is wrong with retraining weekly as a default?
options: Every retrain produces a new model that can be worse and needs the same gate — automated retraining without a gate can ship a regression every Monday
Weekly retraining is too expensive for most teams to afford
Frequent retraining makes the model forget older patterns
Nothing: more frequent retraining is always safer
p14.explanation: Cadence should follow the drift you actually measured, not diligence. And the gate stays: a newer model that does not beat the one in production is not promoted for being newer.

p14.question: When is switching the feature off the right product decision?
options: Never — a launched feature should be improved rather than removed
When the team that built it moves on to another project
When a competitor launches something similar
When the increment no longer covers the monthly cost of owning the model, or the decision it fed no longer exists
p14.explanation: The cost of owning a model is monthly and permanent while the value can fade. Removing a feature whose increment has stopped paying for its machinery is the same arithmetic as module P10's gate, applied a year later.

p15.question: Among an ML feature's four cost lines, which is frequently the largest and scales with volume in the worst way?
options: Inference, because it is charged per call
Human review of the uncertain band, at a real hourly rate
Storage of the training data
The original training run
p15.explanation: Every case routed to a person costs a person's time, and that cost grows linearly with volume with no economy of scale whatsoever. Inference is the line everyone names first and is often an order of magnitude smaller.

p15.question: Why work in cost per decision rather than cost per month?
options: Because finance reports monthly figures anyway
Because cloud providers bill per request
Because it makes the number smaller and easier to get approved
Because it can be set against the value per decision, survives a change in volume, and makes two architectures comparable in a single line
p15.explanation: A monthly lump sum cannot be compared to anything, forecast when volume triples, or defended in a budget review. Per-decision cost does all three, and it is the form in which the expensive-model trap becomes visible.

p15.question: A model is four points better and twenty-five times more expensive per call. What structure usually beats both it and the cheap model?
options: Running both models and averaging their outputs
Using the expensive model only during business hours
A cascade: the cheap model on everything, the expensive one only on the cases the cheap model is unsure about
Negotiating a volume discount on the expensive model
p15.explanation: The cascade reuses module P9's three bands — the middle band can go to a better model before it goes to a human. It typically keeps almost all of the quality for a small fraction of the per-call bill.

p15.question: In the worked photo-moderation example, which block was the largest cost in every one of the three options?
options: The violations that still got through
Inference on the large vision model
Human review of the flagged items
Labelling and the data pipelines
p15.explanation: Between $13,000 and $32,000 a month, against an inference line of $108 to $10,800. That is the finding: the leverage was in catch rate, and the cheap-versus-expensive argument was about the smallest number on the page.

p15.question: Which two cost lines deserve a forecast at ten times today's volume before you commit?
options: Storage and training compute
Per-call model pricing and human review
Labelling and monitoring
The on-call rotation and incident response
p15.explanation: Both grow faster than the business and neither improves with scale. A feature that is comfortable at 9,000 items a day and impossible at 90,000 is not a strategy, and now is when that is cheap to discover.

p16.question: What is the first question in a build-buy-or-call decision, before any price is compared?
options: Whether the vendor's API latency fits our budget
Whether our team has the skills to build it
Whether the capability is a utility the whole industry needs in the same form, or a differentiator whose value comes from our own data
Whether the vendor will commit to a two-year contract
p16.explanation: Getting this axis wrong is expensive in both directions: a year spent building transcription you could have called, or a differentiator handed to a supplier who then sells the same capability to a competitor.

p16.question: Which cost of buying never appears in the quote and limits you permanently?
options: The per-call price once you reach full volume
The ceiling: when the vendor is wrong in a way specific to your business, you cannot fix it — you can only file a request
The engineering time the integration takes
The training your team needs in order to use the API
p16.explanation: Integration and switching costs are painful but finite. The ceiling is permanent: a false-block pattern costing you $30,000 a month becomes an item in somebody else's backlog, prioritised against their other customers.

p16.question: What did general-purpose model APIs change about this decision?
options: They make building in-house obsolete for every capability
They remove the need to measure a baseline
They make buying cheaper than building at any volume
They add a third option — fast, priced per call, and with no moat: excellent for finding out whether the decision matters, poor as a permanent home for a differentiator at scale
p16.explanation: It is module P7's spike with the search removed: you can have the decision live in days and learn whether anyone acts on it. What you do not get is an advantage, because a competitor can call the same model tomorrow.

p16.question: The vendor's deck claims 75% of fraud caught. What is that number?
options: A hypothesis about your data, measured on somebody else's traffic by someone with an interest in the result
A contractual commitment you can hold them to
A lie until proven otherwise
Evidence, as long as a third party audited it
p16.explanation: It is neither a lie nor evidence. Their fraud mix, devices and geography are not yours, and it is entirely normal for a vendor model to land well below its headline on a new customer's traffic — which is what shadow mode is for.

p16.question: When is buying a capability that is genuinely a differentiator an acceptable decision?
options: Never: a differentiator has to be built in-house
When a long contract fixes the price for the whole term
When the arithmetic is large enough to justify it, and your own capability stays alive while your exit stays priced
When the vendor agrees not to serve your competitors
p16.explanation: “It is our differentiator” is not on its own an argument worth hundreds of thousands a year. What makes the trade safe is that it remains reversible — and it stops being safe the moment the in-house model or the priced exit quietly lapses.

p17.question: Why is “we already have the data” not a sufficient reason to train on it?
options: Because purpose limitation means data gathered for one purpose does not automatically become training data for another
Because older data is usually too stale to be useful
Because the data team has to approve every new use
Because storage costs grow with every model trained
p17.explanation: Data collected so a delivery could be completed is not automatically available for pricing. Writing the purpose into the PRD is what makes a later request for a different use a decision rather than a default.

p17.question: The fraud model's measured precision keeps improving month after month. Why is that suspicious?
options: Because precision always degrades in production, so a rise indicates a bug
Because label lag makes any recent measurement unreliable
Because blocked transactions never produce an outcome, so the model is only ever graded on the cases it let through
Because precision cannot be measured without a control group of honest customers
p17.explanation: Rejected applicants never default. The model is being evaluated on a slice of the world it already judged safe, and that slice narrows as the model grows more confident — so the number rises while meaning less.

p17.question: What is the standard instrument for measuring a decision you actually act on?
options: Ask the model for a calibrated confidence and trust it
Survey the affected customers after the fact
Compare against a vendor's benchmark on similar data
Hold out a small random sample from the model's action, let those cases through, and observe what happens
p17.explanation: You cannot reason your way out of missing data. The hold-out costs real money in fraud let through, and that cost is the price of knowing whether the system works — typically a few per cent of what the errors already cost.

p17.question: A thumbs-up widget produces labels for free. What has to be recorded next to that data?
options: The exact time each rating was submitted
That only a particular kind of person presses it, so it is usable for finding patterns and never as a rate
That ratings should be weighted by the customer's lifetime value
That the widget will be removed once enough labels are collected
p17.explanation: Appeals come from sellers who know the process; ratings come from people with a strong opinion. Such labels are genuinely useful for spotting a device type or a city, and dangerous the moment they become the sole measure of anything.

p17.question: Precision will now be computed on the hold-out sample only. What happens to the old series?
options: Delete it, since it was measuring the wrong thing
Recompute it retroactively under the new definition
Report both numbers side by side indefinitely
Leave it on the chart with a line marking the change — a metric that silently changes definition is worse than either version of it
p17.explanation: Anyone reading the chart in six months needs to see that the definition moved and when. Silently swapping the meaning of a line is how an organisation loses the ability to trust its own history.

p18.question: Sellers in one region have photos rejected three times more often. What does that fact establish?
options: That the model is biased against that region
Nothing on its own — a group that genuinely breaks a rule more often will legitimately be rejected more often
That the threshold should be lowered for that region
That the region should be excluded from automation permanently
p18.explanation: Outcome rates and error rates are different questions. The distinction protects you in both directions: it stops a real harm being dismissed as a base-rate difference, and stops a legitimate difference being “fixed” by lowering the bar for one group.

p18.question: How do you actually obtain the wrongful-rejection rate for each group?
options: Take a sample of decisions from each group, strip the group marker, and have senior humans re-review them blind
Compute it from production logs by comparing rejections against appeals
Ask the model for its confidence on each rejected item
Compare the rejection rates and subtract each group's base rate of violations
p18.explanation: Production data does not know which rejections were wrong, so the error rate cannot be computed from it. A blind re-review of a couple of hundred cases per group costs about two days, and there is no way around it.

p18.question: What sets a model's risk tier?
options: The size of the model and how much data it was trained on
Whether the capability was built in-house or bought
The consequence for the person affected — money, access, employment, health
Whether the feature is customer-facing or internal
p18.explanation: The same technique is unremarkable in ranking and heavily regulated in credit. Work the tier out at the PRD stage: its cost is entirely front-loaded, and discovering it at the launch review turns two weeks into a quarter.

p18.question: The disparity is real and traces to an unusual photo background common in that region. Why is a lower threshold for the region the wrong fix?
options: Because per-segment thresholds are difficult to maintain
Because it would push review volume past the team's capacity
Because regulators forbid treating regions differently under any circumstances
Because it hides the error-rate gap by letting genuine violations through there — harming local buyers and the honest sellers who compete with those violations
p18.explanation: The mechanism was the background, not the region. A per-region threshold targets the symptom, calls itself fairness, and quietly transfers the harm to the people in that region who were doing nothing wrong.

p18.question: Rejections in the affected window were wrong. How should the remedy be delivered?
options: Proactively re-review and restore them — waiting for appeals reaches only the sellers who knew how to complain
Through the standard appeal process, which exists precisely for this
By notifying every seller in the region and inviting them to resubmit
By compensating the affected sellers rather than restoring their listings
p18.explanation: An appeals-only remedy reproduces the original unfairness, because the people least able to navigate the process were disproportionately harmed in the first place. Restoring proactively is both the right outcome and the cheaper one to explain.

p19.question: What are the two sections of an honest ML roadmap?
options: Confident and stretch
Must-have and nice-to-have
Committed work with dates, and bets funded to a decision
Model work and platform work
p19.explanation: The labels matter. “Stretch” invites everyone to read it as a soft promise; “funded to a decision” states exactly what has been bought — an answer by a date, not an outcome.

p19.question: What does funding an uncertain bet in tranches actually buy you?
options: It turns “we might waste two quarters” into “we might waste two weeks, several times over”
It reduces the total cost of the project
It lets the team work on several bets at the same time
It removes the need for a stopping criterion
p19.explanation: The mechanism is that the next tranche is not approved in advance. The total cost of a successful bet is unchanged; what changes is the cost of the ones that were never going to work.

p19.question: Why write down the probability you are assuming for each bet?
options: Because the board requires a formal risk register
It makes the portfolio comparable, and over a year of bets it measures your own calibration
Because it protects you if the bet fails
Because the model's confidence should match the plan
p19.explanation: You cannot see that $6M at 30% deserves a cheaper first step than $900K at 50% without the numbers. And a product manager whose 70%s come true roughly 70% of the time is worth far more than one who is always confident.

p19.question: A bet is worth $6M a year, you put it at 30%, and full funding is two quarters for four people. What do you fund?
options: Two quarters: it has the highest expected value on the page
Nothing: 30% is too low to justify the work
One quarter, as a compromise between the value and the odds
Two weeks, to answer the single question the odds depend on — and nothing beyond that
p19.explanation: The highest expected value often belongs to the least likely bet, and that is an argument for a cheap first tranche rather than a big commitment. Two weeks answers whether the data can be joined; after that the bet is re-priced with evidence.

p19.question: You cannot promise an outcome. What does leadership actually need instead?
options: A padded date you are confident of hitting
The best case, so that the budget is approved
A calendar of when you will know, and what each date produces
A range running from best case to worst case
p19.explanation: A board can plan a conversation, a hire and a budget around a date of knowing. It can plan nothing around an accuracy target — and a decision date is a commitment you can actually keep.

p20.question: The defence contains a block on the money. What form does that block have to take?
options: The annual value of the feature
The increment over what happens today, with the baseline measured the same way
The cost of building the model, amortised over the first year
The saving in agent time, before error costs
p20.explanation: A number with no baseline is not a result, and a baseline measured differently is not a comparison. Both halves are needed before the saving means anything to a finance lead.

p20.question: The case claims the model wrongly approves 3.1% against the agents' 4.4%. What makes that comparison legitimate?
options: Agent error rates for refund handling are published industry-wide
The agents' rate is higher, which is the normal expectation
The model's rate was measured on a larger sample
The agents' rate was measured the same way — a blind re-review of the same slice of requests
p20.explanation: “Better than the humans” is the claim most often made without evidence. It only holds when both numbers come from the same instrument on the same cases, which here is a blind re-review.

p20.question: Why does the refund model approve automatically but never deny?
options: The two errors differ in kind: a wrong approval costs the company $28, while a wrong denial takes money from someone who was entitled to it
Because denial would require more accuracy than the model has
Because regulators prohibit automated denials in every jurisdiction
Because denials are rarer and so not worth automating
p20.explanation: When errors differ in kind rather than only in price, the answer is usually not a cleverer threshold but automating one direction. You give up some saving and remove a harm you could not have priced honestly.

p20.question: Every proposal has one number that will not survive scrutiny. What do you do with it?
options: Leave it out — the defence is one page
Present it at the end, once the case has been made
Name it in the first two minutes, together with what you are doing about it
Replace it with a conservative estimate so that nobody queries it
p20.explanation: A finance lead who finds the soft number themselves stops believing the other five. One who hears it from you starts helping you firm it up, which is a much better use of the same forty minutes.

p20.question: What form should “what would change my mind” take?
options: A commitment to revisit the decision every quarter
A number somebody could go and measure: this stops paying at about 10.7%, and we are at 3.1%
A list of the assumptions the case rests on
A promise to stop if the team loses confidence in the model
p20.explanation: A break-even number converts a debate about confidence into a measurement with a distance attached. It also tells the room exactly what the hold-out is for, and why paying for it is not optional.

p21.question: What is an eval?
options: A benchmark score published by the model provider
A held-out test set with labels and a single metric
A survey asking users whether the output was good
A frozen case set, explicit criteria and a grader — closer to a QA test suite than to a machine-learning metric
p21.explanation: And it belongs to the product manager rather than the ML team, because every criterion in it is a decision about what “good” means for this product.

p21.question: Version 1 scores 71% overall, and 6.1% of its drafts promise something the company cannot deliver. What does that demonstrate?
options: That 71% is too low a bar for anything customer-facing
That one overall number hides the failure you care most about, so criteria have to be scored separately
That the rubric's weights need adjusting
That human graders are unreliable at this sample size
p21.explanation: 71% is a respectable-looking score that concealed 366 false promises a day. Averaging a hard requirement into a rubric is how a gate quietly becomes a weight.

p21.question: How should a prompt be treated?
options: As configuration, editable by whoever owns the feature
As documentation describing the model's intended behaviour
As a release: versioned, reviewed and gated by the eval — a wording change is a production deploy
As an internal implementation detail belonging to the ML team
p21.explanation: A prompt encodes policy: what the system may promise, what tone it uses, what it refuses. One edited sentence changes the product for every customer instantly and with no build, which is exactly why it needs the ceremony of a release.

p21.question: The same input produces different outputs each run. What follows for the acceptance criteria?
options: They have to be properties that hold across samples, and each case is run several times
They have to be relaxed until the observed variation fits inside them
They cannot be automated and must be checked by hand every release
The model must be made deterministic before any testing happens
p21.explanation: “Never promises a delivery date” is testable across a thousand samples; “produces this exact paragraph” is a coincidence rather than a criterion. And a failure appearing one time in three is a real failure, not noise.

p21.question: Which failure modes belong in the PRD for an LLM feature?
options: Overfitting to the training data
Point-in-time leakage from a feature that exists only after the decision
Class imbalance in the evaluation set
Confident fabrication, instructions hidden in user-supplied content, and context leaking between customers
p21.explanation: All three are product problems with product defences: grounding in the order record, treating anything a user supplied as data rather than instructions, and a launch check on isolation between customers.

p22.question: What actually changes as a feature moves up the autonomy ladder?
options: Accountability for the outcome moves away from a person who read it
The accuracy the model needs rises proportionally with each rung
The cost per action falls, because no human time is spent
The feature becomes easier to evaluate
p22.explanation: At rung 2 a named employee read the message and sent it. Remove the click and the company is talking to its customers by itself — which is a transfer of responsibility, not a quality improvement.

p22.question: What sets the right rung for a feature?
options: The model's measured accuracy
The number of actions it performs per day
The blast radius: what the worst single run can do, and how many runs happen before a person looks
Whether the team can monitor it in real time
p22.explanation: A 99%-accurate agent with unbounded reach is a worse product than a 90%-accurate one that can only affect one customer per run. Accuracy describes the model; blast radius describes what happens when it is wrong.

p22.question: Why is gating on the model's confidence the wrong design?
options: Because most models do not expose a confidence score
Because confidence varies too much between runs to be a stable gate
Because a confidence gate needs labels that arrive too late to be useful
Because the model is often most fluent exactly where it is inventing — gate on irreversibility, magnitude and bulk instead
p22.explanation: Gate on properties of the action, not of the prediction: can the affected person undo it, does it move money or data outside the company, is it irreversible in practice, is it a bulk action.

p22.question: A four-step agent chain is right 95% of the time at each step. What is the success rate, and what follows?
options: 95%: the steps are independent, so the overall rate is unchanged
81%: one run in five goes wrong somewhere, so the answer is short chains with a cheap verification after each step
99%: errors in separate steps tend to cancel each other out
38%: each step multiplies the error rate rather than the success rate
p22.explanation: And the failures are not spread evenly — they cluster in the unusual cases that most needed a human. A verified step resets the multiplication, which is why the fix is the chain's shape rather than a better model.

p22.question: A four-step agent issued a refund incorrectly. What makes the incident explainable?
options: The full trajectory: every step, tool call and intermediate result, because the real question is which step went wrong
The model version and the final output
The confidence score attached to the decision
The eval suite's score on that ticket type
p22.explanation: Module P13's inputs-and-version logging is not enough once a system takes several steps. Without the trajectory the first serious incident is unexplainable, and an unexplainable incident gets the feature switched off permanently.

p23.question: In an ML strategy, where does a durable advantage come from?
options: Training a larger model than competitors can afford
Owning a large volume of data
The loop: a competitor can call the same model this afternoon, and cannot buy your recorded outcomes
Hiring the strongest ML team on the market
p23.explanation: Volume is not an advantage; data that arises only from running this particular business is. And it compounds only if every automated decision records its own outcome, which is what makes the loop rather than the model the asset.

p23.question: When should shared platform capability be built?
options: Before the first feature, so that it does not have to be retrofitted
When the third feature needs the same thing — by then there is enough variation to fit it and enough consumers to call it a platform
Once the ML team is large enough to maintain it
After a vendor's tooling turns out to be too expensive
p23.explanation: Built for the first feature it is an abstraction over one example; built for the third it fits three real cases. A feature store with no second consumer is not infrastructure, it is a hobby with a budget.

p23.question: Which section do people most often leave out of a twelve-month ML plan?
options: The money attached to each decision
The platform investments
The decision dates for the uncertain bets
What you will not do, and why
p23.explanation: A strategy that excludes nothing has chosen nothing. Naming what you are declining — and the reasoning, such as “both are utilities we would spend a year to catch up on” — is what makes the rest of the page credible.

p23.question: What is wrong with building a capability first and finding the decision it serves later?
options: A capability nobody is waiting for is a sophisticated cost centre, and it takes about two years to admit it
It takes longer than doing it in the other order
It cannot be funded in tranches
Nothing: platform investment has to precede the features that use it
p23.explanation: Every strategy item should be traceable to a decision somebody makes and a cost of getting it wrong. Reversed, the work looks impressive for long enough that nobody wants to be the person who stops it.

p23.question: The delivery advisory earns about $14,000 a year and appears on the strategy page anyway. Why include it?
options: Because every shipped feature has to be listed for completeness
Because listing it justifies continuing to invest in it
Because a strategy that cannot name its smallest result is hiding something
Because small numbers make the large ones look more credible
p23.explanation: It is also being stopped on the same page, which is the point: naming a fourteen-thousand-dollar result and declining to spend another quarter on it is what tells a board that the other numbers were not chosen for effect.
